questions.question_text:
A projectile launched from the origin has $x=10t$ and $y=40t-5t^{2}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres.
Which is the Cartesian equation of its path?

options.why: Replaced $t$ by $x$ in the linear term instead of by $\dfrac{x}{10}$.
Squared only the numerator of $\dfrac{x}{10}$, giving $\dfrac{x^{2}}{10}$ instead of $\dfrac{x^{2}}{100}$.
Both slips: $t$ replaced by $x$ in the linear term and the denominator left unsquared.

questions.question_text:
A projectile launched from the origin follows $y=\dfrac{2}{3}x-\dfrac{1}{90}x^{2}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres.
What is its range?

options.why: Solved $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, giving the horizontal distance to the greatest height rather than the range.
Read the range straight off the denominator of the $x^{2}$ term.
Doubled the landing distance, treating it as the halfway point of the flight.

questions.question_text:
A projectile launched from the origin follows $y=\dfrac{3}{4}x-\dfrac{1}{64}x^{2}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres.
What is its greatest height?

options.why: Gave the horizontal distance to the highest point instead of the height there.
Substituted $x=24$ into $\dfrac{3}{4}x$ only, dropping the $x^{2}$ term.
Substituted the range $x=48$ into $\dfrac{3}{4}x$ instead of using the turning point.

questions.question_text:
A projectile launched from the origin follows $y=\dfrac{7}{6}x-\dfrac{1}{48}x^{2}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres.
What is the direction of motion at $x=48$, to 1 d.p.?

options.why: Ignored the negative gradient, which shows the projectile is descending at that point.
Used $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{6}{5}\right)$, inverting the gradient ratio.
Both slips: the ratio inverted and the descent ignored.

questions.question_text:
A projectile launched from the origin follows $y=\dfrac{5}{4}x-\dfrac{1}{64}x^{2}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres.
What is its height when it has travelled $16\text{ m}$ horizontally?

options.why: Used only the $\dfrac{5}{4}x$ term and left out the $x^{2}$ term.
Added the $x^{2}$ term instead of subtracting it.
Gave the value of the $x^{2}$ term rather than the height.

questions.question_text:
A ball is thrown horizontally at $8\text{ m/s}$ from the top of a cliff.
Taking the point of projection as the origin, up as positive and $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, which is the Cartesian equation of its path?

options.why: Took downwards as positive, although the stem sets up as the positive direction.
Did not square the $8$ when substituting $t=\dfrac{x}{8}$.
Both slips: the denominator left unsquared and the sign of gravity reversed.

questions.question_text:
A projectile leaves the origin with speed $V$ at angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal, so that $x=Vt\cos\alpha$ and $y=Vt\sin\alpha-\dfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}$.
Which is the Cartesian equation of the path?

options.why: Used $t=\dfrac{x}{V}$ in the $t^{2}$ term, so the $\cos^{2}\alpha$ is missing.
Did not divide $V\sin\alpha$ by $V\cos\alpha$, so the linear term keeps only the sine.
Both slips: the sine left undivided and $\cos^{2}\alpha$ missing from the denominator.

questions.question_text:
A projectile is launched from the origin at $V=40\text{ m/s}$ and angle $\theta$, with $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$ and path $y=x\tan\theta-\dfrac{gx^{2}}{2V^{2}}\sec^{2}\theta$.
Its range is $80\text{ m}$.
What are the possible angles of projection, for $0^{\circ}<\theta<90^{\circ}$?

options.why: Gave the values of $2\theta$ without halving them to find $\theta$.
Took only the acute solution of $\sin 2\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and missed the obtuse one.
Halved the angles a second time after already halving $2\theta$.

questions.solution_text:
At $y=0$ with $x\ne 0$, the range is $\dfrac{V^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}$.
$\dfrac{1600\sin 2\theta}{10}=80$
$\sin 2\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$
For $0^{\circ}<2\theta<180^{\circ}$:
$2\theta=30^{\circ}$ or $150^{\circ}$
$\theta=15^{\circ}$ or $75^{\circ}$
